Permutation and bootstrap tests

Source: vignettes/resampling.Rmd
resampling.Rmd

F and t tests rest on the model’s distributional assumptions and, for mixed models, on approximate degrees of freedom. With few experimental units, skewed residuals or a GLMM, resampling tests are a useful check. predictmeans has:

  • permmodels(): permutation tests of the terms and coefficients of lm, aov, glm, gls, lme, lmer, glmer and glmmTMB models;
  • permlmer() (also as permglmer() and permglmmTMB()) and permanova.lmer(): permutation likelihood-ratio tests comparing two nested mixed models, including tests of random effects;
  • permindex(): permutations restricted by the design (within blocks, of whole plots), for randomisation tests;
  • bootmodels(): parametric bootstrap tests for lmer and glmer models.

The results of permmodels() and bootmodels() can be passed to predictmeans() and contrastmeans() (argument permlist), which then give resampling p-values for pairwise comparisons and contrasts.

The examples below use 99 to 999 resamples so that they run quickly; use 999 or more in practice. The smallest p-value possible is 1/(number of resamples + 1). ncore sets the number of cores used for refits (ncore = 1 here, as for CRAN checks); seed makes the results reproducible without changing your own random number stream.

library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ nitro * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)

How the data are permuted

permmodels() has two schemes.

  • Freedman–Lane (method = "freedman-lane"; the default, through method = "auto"). For each test, the model without the tested term (for a pair of means: with the two means equal) gives fitted values and residuals; the residuals are permuted and added back to those fitted values, and the statistic is computed again (Freedman and Lane 1983). The other terms keep their effects, so each test is of its own term. For linear mixed models the residuals are decorrelated with the symmetric square root of their covariance before they are permuted and correlated again after, and the model is refitted to each permuted data set, so its variance parameters are estimated again each time (one set of refits per term). refit = FALSE instead fixes the covariance of the data at the fit, which turns the model into a linear model with no refits: much faster, but slightly liberal when the variance parameters rest on few units (whole plots with few blocks: 8.6% instead of 5% in a simulation study, against 5.0% with refits). GLMs and GLMMs are first linearised at the fit (working response and working variances on the link scale); a GLMM is then treated as its working linear mixed model and refitted in the same way.
  • Raw (method = "raw", the scheme of predictmeans 1.x). The response (lm, glm) or the fitted values together with the decorrelated residuals (mixed models) are permuted, and the model is refitted to each permuted data set. The refits are kept in permlist. This scrambles the effects of all the terms at once, so it tests the global null hypothesis; with a covariate that has extreme values and is related to the tested term it rejected true null hypotheses too often (6–7% at the 5% level, against 4–5% for Freedman–Lane, in a simulation study; Anderson and Legendre 1999 found the same for linear models).
perm <- permmodels(fm, nperm = 199, seed = 1, ncore = 1)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>                            Estimate Std. Error t value Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)                 80.0000     9.1070  8.7844           NA
#> nitro0.2                    18.5000     7.6829  2.4079        0.025
#> nitro0.4                    34.6667     7.6829  4.5122        0.005
#> nitro0.6                    44.8333     7.6829  5.8354        0.005
#> VarietyMarvellous            6.6667     9.7150  0.6862        0.545
#> VarietyVictory              -8.5000     9.7150 -0.8749        0.410
#> nitro0.2:VarietyMarvellous   3.3333    10.8653  0.3068        0.765
#> nitro0.4:VarietyMarvellous  -4.1667    10.8653 -0.3835        0.715
#> nitro0.6:VarietyMarvellous  -4.6667    10.8653 -0.4295        0.645
#> nitro0.2:VarietyVictory     -0.3333    10.8653 -0.0307        0.990
#> nitro0.4:VarietyVictory      4.6667    10.8653  0.4295        0.670
#> nitro0.6:VarietyVictory      2.1667    10.8653  0.1994        0.885
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of t test is obtained using '199' Freedman-Lane permutations.
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#> Type I F tests (Freedman-Lane permutations; the model refitted to each permuted data set)
#>               Df F value Perm_p_value
#> nitro          3 37.6857        0.005
#> Variety        2  1.4853        0.260
#> nitro:Variety  6  0.3028        0.925
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of F test is obtained using '199' Freedman-Lane permutations.

For lm, aov, lme and gls models the tables are the model’s own tests with a Perm_p_value column; for the other classes they show the statistics that were permuted (Wald t and F with the covariance of the data fixed at the fit).

fm_cars <- lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
permmodels(fm_cars, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)   33.9908     1.8878 18.0056   0.0000           NA
#> wt            -3.2056     0.7539 -4.2521   0.0002        0.001
#> factor(cyl)6  -4.2556     1.3861 -3.0702   0.0047        0.009
#> factor(cyl)8  -6.0709     1.6523 -3.6742   0.0010        0.003
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of t test is obtained using '999' Freedman-Lane permutations.
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#> Anova Table (Type II tests)
#> 
#>  Response: mpg
#>               Sum Sq Df F value Pr(>F) Perm_p_value
#> wt          118.2039  1 18.0801 0.0002        0.001
#> factor(cyl)  95.2633  2  7.2856 0.0028        0.005
#> Residuals   183.0586 28                            
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of F test is obtained using '999' Freedman-Lane permutations.

Pairwise comparisons and contrasts

The same permutations give p-values for pairwise comparisons, in the pairs table and the legacy p-value matrix. With Freedman–Lane each pair is tested with its own reduced model, in which that pair’s means are equal, so its p-value does not depend on the other means:

pm <- predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = perm, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE, ncore = 1)
pm$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "statistic", "p.value", "p.method")]
#>   level1 level2   estimate statistic p.value    p.method
#> 1      0    0.2 -19.500000 -4.396098   0.005 permutation
#> 2      0    0.4 -34.833333 -7.852859   0.005 permutation
#> 3    0.2    0.4 -15.333333 -3.456761   0.005 permutation
#> 4      0    0.6 -44.000000 -9.919400   0.005 permutation
#> 5    0.2    0.6 -24.500000 -5.523302   0.005 permutation
#> 6    0.4    0.6  -9.166667 -2.066542   0.055 permutation

and for contrasts:

cm <- contrast_family(Kmatrix(fm, "nitro"), "trt.vs.ctrl")
contrastmeans(fm, "nitro", ctrmatrix = cm, permlist = perm)[[1]]
#>         Estimate Std. Error t value Permuted Pr(>|t|) lower.CL upper.CL
#> 0.2 - 0  19.5000     4.4358  4.3961             0.005  11.2629  27.7371
#> 0.4 - 0  34.8333     4.4358  7.8529             0.005  26.8245  42.8422
#> 0.6 - 0  44.0000     4.4358  9.9194             0.005  35.5097  52.4903
#> attr(,"Note")
#> [1] "The permuted p-value is obtained using '199' permutations."

With method = "raw" all pairs use the same refits. adj adjusts the permutation p-values with any p.adjust() method or "sidak", and with the max-|t| method of Westfall and Young (1993), which uses the correlation between the comparisons: adj = "tukey" (or "mvt") compares each pair’s |t| with the largest |t| of the family in each permuted data set (a permutation Tukey test), and adj = "westfall" does the same step by step, which is more powerful. In a simulation study this kept the familywise error rate as Tukey’s test does.

pmw <- predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = perm, adj = "westfall", plot = FALSE,
                    prtnum = FALSE, ncore = 1)
pmw$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "p.value", "p.adj")]
#>   level1 level2 p.value p.adj
#> 1      0    0.2   0.005 0.005
#> 2      0    0.4   0.005 0.005
#> 3    0.2    0.4   0.005 0.010
#> 4      0    0.6   0.005 0.005
#> 5    0.2    0.6   0.005 0.005
#> 6    0.4    0.6   0.055 0.055

With a permlist, the observed t statistics use the unadjusted covariance (no Kenward–Roger adjustment), as the permuted ones do.

GLMs and GLMMs

For GLMs and GLMMs permmodels() works on the working (link) scale, with the dispersion estimated from the working residuals, which makes it much less sensitive to overdispersion than the likelihood-ratio test. For the clinical trial data (a binomial GLMM):

data(Clinical)
fm_clin <- glmer(cbind(Favorable, Total - Favorable) ~ Treatment + (1 | Clinic),
                 family = binomial, data = Clinical)
perm_clin <- permmodels(fm_clin, nperm = 199, seed = 1, ncore = 1)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>               Estimate Std. Error t value Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)    -1.1399     0.5591 -2.0389           NA
#> Treatmentdrug   0.7207     0.3070  2.3474        0.075
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of t test is obtained using '199' Freedman-Lane permutations.
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#> Type I F tests on the working (link) scale (Freedman-Lane permutations; the working linear mixed model refitted to each permuted data set)
#>           Df F value Perm_p_value
#> Treatment  1  5.5102        0.075
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of F test is obtained using '199' Freedman-Lane permutations.

Testing random effects: permlmer()

permlmer() compares two nested mixed models with a permutation likelihood-ratio test (Lee and Braun 2012). This is useful for random effects, where the usual chi-square reference distribution is wrong because the null value of a variance lies on the boundary. Does the slope for Days vary between subjects?

fm1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
fm0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
permlmer(fm0, fm1, nperm = 99, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
#> Data: sleepstudy
#> Models:
#> lmer0: Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject)
#> lmer1: Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject)
#>       npar    AIC    BIC  logLik -2*log(L)  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) Perm-p
#> lmer0    4 1794.5 1807.2 -893.23    1786.5                            
#> lmer1    6 1755.6 1774.8 -871.81    1743.6 42.837  2   4.99e-10   0.01

For GLMMs (glmer or glmmTMB, also as permglmer() and permglmmTMB()) the same is done on the working scale. For 0/1 responses, where the working scale fails with rare events or tiny clusters, randomised quantile residuals are permuted instead and the GLMMs refitted (method = "quantile", chosen automatically). Do tick counts vary between locations, beyond the variation between broods?

gm1 <- glmer(TICKS ~ YEAR + scale(HEIGHT) + (1 | BROOD), family = poisson,
             data = lme4::grouseticks)
gm2 <- update(gm1, . ~ . + (1 | LOCATION))
permglmer(gm1, gm2, nperm = 99, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
#> Data: lme4::grouseticks
#> Models:
#> m0: TICKS ~ YEAR + scale(HEIGHT) + (1 | BROOD)
#> m1: TICKS ~ YEAR + scale(HEIGHT) + (1 | BROOD) + (1 | LOCATION)
#>    npar    AIC    BIC  logLik -2*log(L)  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) Perm-p
#> m0    5 1988.1 2008.1 -989.04    1978.1                            
#> m1    6 1987.9 2011.9 -987.94    1975.9 2.1992  1    0.13809   0.08

permanova.lmer() applies the same test to each fixed term of an lmer or glmer model in turn (Type I, II or III), for an ANOVA table with permutation p-values.

Permutations restricted by the design: permindex()

In a designed experiment the randomisation defines which permutations are possible: treatments are randomised within blocks, whole-plot treatments to whole plots. permindex() gives such permutations, and permmodels() and permlmer() use them through perms (a randomisation test):

fm_rcb <- lm(yield ~ Block + nitro, data = Oats)
idx <- permindex(Oats, block = "Block", nsim = 999, seed = 1)
permmodels(fm_rcb, perms = idx)$ANOVA
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)  79.3889     3.7668 21.0759   0.0000           NA
#> Block.L      29.4823     4.6134  6.3906   0.0000        0.069
#> Block.Q      20.0124     4.6134  4.3379   0.0001        1.000
#> Block.C       5.3728     4.6134  1.1646   0.2486        0.001
#> Block^4       4.7718     4.6134  1.0343   0.3049        1.000
#> Block^5      -1.2651     4.6134 -0.2742   0.7848        0.001
#> nitro0.2     19.5000     5.3271  3.6605   0.0005        0.002
#> nitro0.4     34.8333     5.3271  6.5389   0.0000        0.001
#> nitro0.6     44.0000     5.3271  8.2597   0.0000        0.001
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of t test is obtained using '999' Freedman-Lane permutations.
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#>  Response: yield
#>           Df   Sum Sq   Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) Perm_p_value
#> Block      5 15875.28 3175.0556 12.4317      0            1
#> nitro      3 20020.50 6673.5000 26.1297      0        0.001
#> Residuals 63 16090.17  255.3995                            
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of F test is obtained using '999' Freedman-Lane permutations.
#>           Df   Sum Sq   Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) Perm_p_value
#> Block      5 15875.28 3175.0556 12.4317      0            1
#> nitro      3 20020.50 6673.5000 26.1297      0        0.001
#> Residuals 63 16090.17  255.3995

Parametric bootstrap: bootmodels()

bootmodels() simulates new responses from the model fitted without its fixed effects (an intercept and the same random effects: the global null hypothesis), refits the full model to each and compares the statistics. For the clinical trial data:

boot <- bootmodels(fm_clin, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) Boot_p_value
#> (Intercept)    -1.1965     0.5529 -2.1641   0.0305           NA
#> Treatmentdrug   0.7382     0.3004  2.4575   0.0140         0.03
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#>           npar Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Boot_p_value
#> Treatment    1 6.2054  6.2054  6.2054         0.03
#> 
#> Note: Boot_p_value is from '99' parametric bootstrap samples under the global null model.

Its result is used as a permlist; the pairs table then says "bootstrap":

pmb <- predictmeans(fm_clin, "Treatment", permlist = boot, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE,
                    ncore = 1)
pmb$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "p.value", "p.method")]
#>    level1 level2   estimate p.value  p.method
#> 1 control   drug -0.7382041    0.03 bootstrap

Unequal variances: robust = TRUE

No permutation scheme repairs a variance model that is wrong: when groups have very different error variances and the model assumes them equal, the F test and the permutation tests above all reject true null hypotheses far too often (about 20% at the 5% level in our simulations with group SDs 3, 1, 1). For lm, aov and glm models, robust = TRUE uses heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) t and F statistics and flips the signs of the reduced model’s residuals at random instead of permuting them (a wild bootstrap), so each residual keeps its own variance:

mt <- transform(mtcars, cyl = factor(cyl))
fm_mt <- lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mt)
permmodels(fm_mt, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1, robust = TRUE)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects (robust standard errors):
#>             Estimate Robust SE t value Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)  33.9908    2.1414 15.8734           NA
#> wt           -3.2056    0.7548 -4.2467        0.001
#> cyl6         -4.2556    1.2893 -3.3007        0.003
#> cyl8         -6.0709    1.6077 -3.7761        0.004
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of robust t test is obtained using '999' sign flips of the Freedman-Lane residuals (wild bootstrap).
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#> Type II robust (HC3) Wald F tests (Freedman-Lane residuals, sign flips)
#>     Df F value Perm_p_value
#> wt   1 18.0348        0.001
#> cyl  2  7.1814        0.007
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of robust F test is obtained using '999' sign flips of the Freedman-Lane residuals (wild bootstrap).

Pairs and contrasts from this result use the robust statistics and robust standard errors. For mixed models, model the variances instead (e.g. lme(..., weights = varIdent())) and use permmodels() on that model.

More from the permutations: permstats() and permcombine()

permmodels() keeps the permuted statistics. permstats() turns them into a standardised effect size for each term and coefficient, and checks the parametric test against them: param.size is the proportion of permuted data sets (in which the term has no effect) where the parametric test rejects at level. Near level, the parametric test suits these data; well above it, its p-values are too small here.

p_mpg <- permmodels(fm_mt, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1, prt = FALSE)
permstats(p_mpg)
#>           statistic df1 df2      p.param p.perm       ses param.size
#> wt        18.080056   1  28 0.0002130435  0.001 11.695665 0.04904905
#> cyl        7.285567   2  28 0.0028353022  0.005  4.622323 0.05705706
#> coef:wt    4.252065   1  28 0.0002130435  0.001  5.599425 0.04904905
#> coef:cyl6  3.070244   1  28 0.0047178339  0.009  3.291703 0.05905906
#> coef:cyl8  3.674214   1  28 0.0009991893  0.003  4.186066 0.05405405

When the same model is fitted to several responses measured on the same units (traits, time points), results made with the same permutations (same rows, seed and nperm) can be combined. permcombine() gives, for each term, one p-value for “no effect on any response” (Fisher’s or Tippett’s combination; Pesarin and Salmaso 2010) and p-values adjusted for testing every response (min-p; Westfall and Young 1993). The responses’ correlation is kept by the shared permutations, without a multivariate model.

p_qsec <- permmodels(lm(qsec ~ wt + cyl, data = mt), nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1,
                     prt = FALSE)
permcombine(mpg = p_mpg, qsec = p_qsec)
#>             mpg  qsec combined adj.mpg adj.qsec
#> wt        0.001 0.002    0.001   0.002    0.003
#> cyl       0.005 0.002    0.002   0.008    0.004
#> coef:wt   0.001 0.002    0.001   0.002    0.003
#> coef:cyl6 0.009 0.002    0.002   0.016    0.003
#> coef:cyl8 0.003 0.002    0.003   0.004    0.003

For many comparisons within one response, such as a treatment difference at each of several time points, contrastmeans(..., permlist = , adj = "westfall") gives the max-statistic (step-down max-|t|) adjustment over the time points.

Which to use

Model Terms, coefficients, pairs, contrasts Random effects, nested models
lm, aov permmodels() (Freedman–Lane) —
glm permmodels() (Freedman–Lane on the working scale) —
lmer, lme, gls permmodels() (Freedman–Lane with refits); or the Kenward–Roger F test permlmer()
glmer, glmmTMB permmodels() (Freedman–Lane on the working scale, with refits) permlmer(): working scale; quantile residuals for 0/1 responses
designed experiments permmodels(perms = permindex(...)) for a randomisation test
lm, glm with unequal variances permmodels(robust = TRUE) (HC3 statistics, sign flips)
several responses, same units permcombine() of permmodels() results with the same seed
  • With large samples and well-behaved residuals the F and t tests (with Kenward–Roger df for lmer) agree closely with these, at a fraction of the time.
  • bootmodels() simulates from the global null model; it is useful as a check for GLMMs and very small samples.
  • The choices come from simulation studies of the type I error and power of each scheme (in the package sources: dev/permutation-plan.md and dev/sim-study/).

References

Davidson, R. and Flachaire, E. (2008). The wild bootstrap, tamed at last. Journal of Econometrics 146, 162–169.

DiCiccio, C. J. and Romano, J. P. (2017). Robust permutation tests for correlation and regression coefficients. Journal of the American Statistical Association 112, 1211–1220.

Pesarin, F. and Salmaso, L. (2010). Permutation Tests for Complex Data: Theory, Applications and Software. Wiley.

Anderson, M. J. and Legendre, P. (1999). An empirical comparison of permutation methods for tests of partial regression coefficients in a linear model. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation 62, 271–303.

Freedman, D. and Lane, D. (1983). A nonstochastic interpretation of reported significance levels. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 1, 292–298.

Dunn, P. K. and Smyth, G. K. (1996). Randomized quantile residuals. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 5, 236–244.

Lee, O. E. and Braun, T. M. (2012). Permutation tests for random effects in linear mixed models. Biometrics 68, 486–493.

Westfall, P. H. and Young, S. S. (1993). Resampling-Based Multiple Testing. Wiley.
